claim: The coordination of activity across neocortical areas is essential for mammalian brain function.
source: The coordination of activity across neocortical areas is essential for mammalian brain function.
evidence: This is a general statement about brain function that draws from established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Sensory perception, fine voluntary motor control, and higher cognitive functions depend on neural dynamics in the mammalian neocortex.
source: Sensory perception, fine voluntary motor control, and higher cognitive functions depend on neural dynamics in the mammalian neocortex, which itself relies on the exchange of information between cortical areas through both bottom-up (feedforward) and top-down (feedback) neuronal pathways across the cortical hierarchy (Bressler and Menon, 2010; Buschman and Miller, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cortico-cortical connections are formed between columnar microcircuits via long-range axons of pyramidal neurons in superficial layer 2/3 (L2/3) and deeper layer 5.
source: Cortico-cortical connections are formed between columnar microcircuits via long-range axons of pyramidal neurons in superficial layer 2/3 (L2/3) and deeper layer 5.
evidence: This is a statement about established anatomical knowledge of cortical connectivity.

claim: A given cortical area typically establishes connectivity patterns not only with one particular area but with multiple target areas in a distributed and often reciprocal fashion.
source: A given cortical area typically establishes connectivity patterns not only with one particular area but with multiple target areas in a distributed and often reciprocal fashion (Markov et al., 2013; Oh et al., 2014; Zingg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on cortical connectivity patterns.

claim: The multi-area two-photon microscope enables simultaneous scanning of two sub-areas within a relatively large field of view.
source: We built a two-photon microscope capable of simultaneous scanning of two sub-areas within a relatively large field of view (FOV), enabling one to freely and independently position the sub-areas in order to select appropriate imaging spots.
evidence: This describes the technical capability of the microscope built by the authors.

claim: The microscope uses a 16x water-immersion Nikon objective (NA 0.8) that supports imaging in a FOV of 1.8-mm maximum side length with cellular resolution.
source: Specifically, we chose a 16x water-immersion Nikon objective (NA 0.8) as core element, which supports imaging in a FOV of 1.8-mm maximum side length with cellular resolution (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by the description of the microscope components and referenced figures showing the imaging capability.

claim: The two excitation beams are delayed by 6.25 ns, half of the inter-pulse interval, to interlace the two pulse trains.
source: We split laser light from a Ti:sapphire laser (80 MHz pulse repetition rate) into two excitation beams using a 50:50 beam splitter and delayed the laser pulse train of one beam by 6.25 ns, half of the inter-pulse interval, to interlace the two pulse trains so that the two sub-areas receive alternating laser excitation pulses.
evidence: This describes the technical implementation of the temporal multiplexing approach.

claim: For typical 2–4 ns fluorescence lifetimes of fluorescent proteins, the 6.25-ns time windows are sufficiently long to capture mainly fluorescence photons generated by the last excitation pulse.
source: For typical 2–4 ns fluorescence lifetimes of fluorescent proteins (Akerboom et al., 2013), the 6.25-ns time windows are sufficiently long to capture mainly fluorescence photons generated by the last excitation pulse.
evidence: This is based on known fluorescence lifetimes from cited literature and inference about the temporal separation.

claim: S1ND and S2S1 neurons showed better overall GLM fits to behavioral parameters compared to their neuronal counterparts in their respective areas.
source: S1ND and S2S1 neurons showed better overall GLM fits to these behavioral parameters compared to their neuronal counterparts in their respective areas (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; S1ND vs. S1S2,p<0.002; S2ND vs. S2S1,p<0.005, KS-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the GLM fits shown in the referenced figures.

claim: S2S1 and S1ND neurons showed higher GLM coefficients for whisker-touch onset than their within-area counterparts.
source: Further analysis of fits to specific regressors revealed that S2S1 and S1ND neurons showed higher GLM coefficients for whisker-touch onset than their within-area counterparts (Figure 3D; S1ND vs. S1S2, p<0.05; S2ND vs. S2S1, p<0.005, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of GLM coefficients shown in Figure 3D.

claim: S2S1 neurons showed higher GLM coefficients than S2ND neurons for whisking and licking onset.
source: While no specific differences were observed for cell classes in S1, S2S1 neurons showed higher GLM coefficients than S2ND neurons for whisking and licking onset (p<0.001, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of GLM coefficients.

claim: A larger fraction of S2S1 neurons (72%) was able to discriminate Hit vs. CR trials above chance compared to other neuronal classes.
source: Single-cell ROC analysis of Hit vs. CR trials revealed that a larger fraction of S2S1 neurons compared to other neuronal classes (72%) was able to discriminate these two conditions above chance (Figure 3E; p<0.002, χ2 test).
evidence: This is supported by ROC analysis data shown in Figure 3E with statistical testing.

claim: A larger fraction of S2S1 neurons (50%) was able to discriminate FA vs. CR trials above chance.
source: To disambiguate these possibilities, we also performed ROC analysis of FA vs. CR trials, which were previously shown to consist of similar whisking and sensory conditions (Chen et al., 2015). Again, a larger fraction of S2S1 neurons (50%) was able to discriminate these two conditions above chance (p<0.05, χ2 test), suggesting that this greater discrimination power of S2S1 neurons represents decision- or action-related information.
evidence: This is supported by ROC analysis with statistical testing and citation to previous work.

claim: S2S1 neurons were not more likely to discriminate P280 vs. P1200 textures on CR trials compared to other cell types.
source: As an additional control, we assessed sensory-related responses by ROC analysis of P280 vs. P1200 textures on CR trials and found that S2S1 neurons were not more likely to discriminate these trial types compared to other cell types (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by ROC analysis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: LDCCS1:S2 increased immediately following whisker-touch onset for both Hit and CR trials.
source: We termed this cross-areal correlation LDCCS1:S2, which during task performance increased immediately following whisker-touch onset for both Hit and CR trials.
evidence: This describes the observed temporal dynamics of cross-areal correlation.

claim: 500 ms after touch onset, LDCCS1:S2 remained elevated for Hit trials relative to CR trials.
source: 500 ms after touch onset, however, LDCCS1:S2 remained elevated for Hit trials relative to CR trials (Figure 5B, p<0.05, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the cross-areal correlation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The time point of LDCCS1:S2 divergence between Hit and CR trials corresponded to the average delay of licking onset from whisker-touch onset (mean reaction time: 524 ± 5 ms for Hit trials).
source: The time point of this divergence corresponded to the average delay of licking onset from whisker-touch onset (mean reaction time: 524 ± 5 ms for Hit trials; Figure 5C) (Chen et al., 2013b; 2015).
evidence: This is supported by measurement of reaction times shown in Figure 5C and cited previous work.

claim: LDCCS1:S2 increased and peaked at licking onset and remained elevated thereafter when Hit trials were re-aligned to licking onset.
source: LDCCS1:S2 increased and peaked at licking onset and remained elevated thereafter, further suggesting that coordination of activity across S1 and S2 could be associated with such behavior.
evidence: This describes the temporal relationship between cross-areal correlation and licking behavior.

claim: LDCCS1:S2 was higher for FA compared to CR trials both prior to and following whisker-touch onset.
source: We found LDCCS1:S2 was higher for FA compared to CR trials both prior to and following whisker-touch onset, (p<0.05, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of cross-areal correlation data.

claim: LDCCS1:S2 showed an increased level prior to whisker-touch onset specifically for FA trials in which licking preceded whisker-touch onset.
source: LDCCS1:S2 showed an increased level prior to whisker-touch onset specifically for the subset of trials with early licking (Figure 5G,p<0.05, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of cross-areal correlation data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: High-amplitude whisking trials were associated with higher LDCCS1:S2 prior to and after whisker-touch onset when compared to low-amplitude whisking trials.
source: Similar to the results for licking behavior, high-amplitude whisking trials were associated with higher LDCCS1:S2 prior to and after whisker-touch onset when compared to low-amplitude whisking trials (Figure 5I,p<0.02, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures), demonstrating another motor-related component of S1-S2 coordination.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of cross-areal correlation data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Stimulation with distinct textures did not result in elevated LDCCS1:S2.
source: By using LDA for other pairs of trial conditions, we found that stimulation with distinct textures did not result in elevated LDCCS1:S2, suggesting that S1-S2 coordination is not stimulus-specific (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of cross-areal correlation for different texture conditions shown in the referenced figures.

claim: S1S2 and S2S1 neurons especially contributed to LDCCS1:S2 upon licking onset on Hit trials.
source: However, analysis of Hit trials after aligning to licking onset revealed a negative dip in △LDCCS1:S2 when shuffling projection neurons, indicating that S1S2 and S2S1 neurons especially contributed to LDCCS1:S2 upon licking onset (Figure 6B, p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the trial-shuffling experiment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: S1S2 and S2S1 neurons significantly contributed to LDCCS1:S2 in high-amplitude whisking trials following but not preceding whisker-touch onset.
source: We first measured △LDCCS1:S2 from population responses projected onto the high- vs. low-whisking amplitude axis (for CR trials) and found that S1S2 and S2S1 neurons significantly contributed to LDCCS1:S2 in high-amplitude whisking trials following but not preceding whisker-touch onset (Figure 6C, p<0.02, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the trial-shuffling experiment shown in Figure 6C.

claim: S2S1 and S1S2 neurons did not specially contribute to LDCCS1:S2 for FA trials in which licking onset preceded whisker-touch onset.
source: Similarly, analysis of FA vs. CR trials showed that S2S1 and S1S2 neurons did not specially contribute to LDCCS1:S2 for FA trials in which licking onset preceded whisker-touch onset (Figure 6D), but they did so for trials in which licking onset followed whisker-touch onset (Figure 6E, p<0.02, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the trial-shuffling experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: S2S1 and S1S2 neurons contributed to LDCCS1:S2 for FA trials in which licking onset followed whisker-touch onset.
source: Similarly, analysis of FA vs. CR trials showed that S2S1 and S1S2 neurons did not specially contribute to LDCCS1:S2 for FA trials in which licking onset preceded whisker-touch onset (Figure 6D), but they did so for trials in which licking onset followed whisker-touch onset (Figure 6E, p<0.02, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the trial-shuffling experiment shown in Figure 6E.

claim: △LDCCS1:S2 decreased when trial-shuffling S1S2 and S2S1 neurons compared to S1ND and S2ND neurons following whisker-touch onset on CR trials.
source: In line with this notion, further analysis showed that △LDCCS1:S2 decreased when trial-shuffling S1S2 and S2S1 neurons compared to S1ND and S2ND neurons following whisker-touch onset on CR trials, when licking behavior is absent (Figure 6F, p<0.02, one-way ANOVA with repeated measures).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the trial-shuffling experiment shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The specific contribution of projection neurons mutually connecting S1 and S2 could reflect sensory- rather than motor-related activity.
source: These findings indicate that while licking and whisking behavior is associated with correlations in population responses across S1 and S2, any special contribution of S1S2 and S2S1 neurons to this coordination depends on the presence of sensory stimulus, thus occurring after the whisker-touch onset. Hence, the specific contribution of projection neurons mutually connecting S1 and S2 could reflect sensory- rather than motor-related activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of results from the trial-shuffling experiments.

claim: Direct cortico-cortical interactions through S1S2 and S2S1 neurons reflect exchange of sensory or decision information rather than motor information.
source: These results demonstrate that direct cortico-cortical interactions through S1S2 and S2S1 neurons reflect exchange of sensory or decision information rather than motor information.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of results across multiple experiments.

claim: Population activity across S1 and S2 is coordinated during relevant task periods in a behavior-dependent manner.
source: While the acquisition rate of the imaging system and the kinetics of the expressed calcium indicator (Chen et al., 2013b) used in this study precludes our ability to capture the 4–10 ms spike latencies reported across mouse cortical areas (Ferezou et al., 2007) for examining spike-timing and monosynaptic relationship of long-range cortical dynamics, we nevertheless observe that population activity across S1 and S2 is coordinated during relevant task periods in a behavior-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by the data presented.

claim: Inter-areal coordination is associated with both goal-directed licking as well as whisking behavior and can occur independent of sensory stimuli.
source: Specifically, through the analysis of correlated population responses across S1 and S2 along multiple LDA axes, we find that inter-areal coordination is associated with both goal-directed licking as well as whisking behavior and that it can occur independent of sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the LDA analysis across different behavioral conditions.

claim: In the absence of tactile stimuli, S1S2 and S2S1 neurons do not show a special contribution to motor-related coordination.
source: In the absence of tactile stimuli, S1S2 and S2S1 neurons do not show a special contribution to motor-related coordination, suggesting that this coordination does not necessarily reflect direct cortico-cortical interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the trial-shuffling results for motor-related conditions without sensory stimulation.

claim: S1 and S2 receive common input from M1 and POm, conveying efferent and re-afferent motor information.
source: S1 and S2 receive common input from M1 and POm, conveying efferent and re-afferent motor information (Deschenes et al., 1998; Suter and Shepherd, 2015), and are additionally coupled by thalamic relays through POm (Theyel et al., 2010) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about anatomical connectivity.

claim: S1 and S2 are additionally coupled by thalamic relays through POm.
source: S1 and S2 receive common input from M1 and POm, conveying efferent and re-afferent motor information (Deschenes et al., 1998; Suter and Shepherd, 2015), and are additionally coupled by thalamic relays through POm (Theyel et al., 2010) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on cited literature about anatomical connectivity.

claim: Motor-related S1 and S2 coordination could be a result of common drive or cortico-thalamocortical pathways through M1 and POm.
source: We speculate that motor-related S1 and S2 coordination could be a result of common drive or cortico-thalamocortical pathways through these shared areas.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results based on known anatomy.

claim: The contribution of identified S1S2 and S2S1 neurons to inter-areal coordination is most prominent when sensory stimuli and motor behavior are paired.
source: In contrast, we find a special contribution of identified S1S2 and S2S1 neurons to inter-areal coordination occurring during whisker-texture touch, indicating that their participation particularly depends on sensory stimuli. This contribution is most prominent when sensory stimuli and motor behavior are paired, such as upon licking onset on Hit trials, which further suggests that such cortico-cortical interactions could be involved in a form of 'active sensation'.
evidence: This is based on the pattern of results from the trial-shuffling experiments.

claim: Cortico-cortical interactions between S1 and S2 could be involved in a form of 'active sensation'.
source: This contribution is most prominent when sensory stimuli and motor behavior are paired, such as upon licking onset on Hit trials, which further suggests that such cortico-cortical interactions could be involved in a form of 'active sensation'.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The findings provide the first direct evidence for a unique contribution of direct cortico-cortical interactions over other sources of correlated activity across S1 and S2.
source: Our findings provide the first direct evidence for a unique contribution of direct cortico-cortical interactions over other sources of correlated activity across these areas.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: The division between direct and indirect interactions along sensory and motor parameters is in line with theories that indirect cortico-thalamocortical pathways are more involved in relaying motor, rather than sensory, signals.
source: The division between direct and indirect interactions along sensory and motor parameters, respectively, is in line with theories that indirect cortico-thalamocortical pathways are more involved in relaying motor, rather than sensory, signals (Sherman and Guillery, 2011).
evidence: This relates the findings to existing theoretical frameworks cited from the literature.

claim: S2S1 neurons exhibit prominent licking and decision-related activity.
source: We find that S2S1 neurons exhibit prominent licking and decision-related activity, which is in line with recent evidence that behavior-related activity in S1 can be inherited from S2 (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the GLM and ROC analysis results and supported by cited literature.

claim: Behavior-related activity in S1 can be inherited from S2.
source: We find that S2S1 neurons exhibit prominent licking and decision-related activity, which is in line with recent evidence that behavior-related activity in S1 can be inherited from S2 (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on cited literature.

claim: Coordinated activity between S1S2 and S2S1 neurons during texture discrimination may reflect sensory processing involved in decision making.
source: Coordinated activity between S1S2 and S2S1 neurons during texture discrimination may reflect sensory processing involved in several functions. One function may be associated with decision making, as exemplified by correlations increasing upon whisker touch onset and peaking upon licking onset on Hit trials.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed coordination.

claim: Coordinated activity between S1S2 and S2S1 neurons may be associated with the reinforcement of particular aspects of the sensory signal through goal-directed learning.
source: Another function may be associated with the reinforcement of particular aspects of the sensory signal that might strengthen or stabilize sensory representations through goal-directed learning, exemplified by the persistent coordinated activity after licking onset on Hit trials (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed coordination, supported by citation.

claim: The multi-area two-photon microscope has a maximum FOV side length of 1.8 mm.
source: Specifically, we chose a 16x water-immersion Nikon objective (NA 0.8) as core element, which supports imaging in a FOV of 1.8-mm maximum side length with cellular resolution (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Video 1).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the microscope supported by figures.

claim: The microscope uses a Ti:sapphire laser with 80 MHz pulse repetition rate.
source: We split laser light from a Ti:sapphire laser (80 MHz pulse repetition rate) into two excitation beams using a 50:50 beam splitter and delayed the laser pulse train of one beam by 6.25 ns, half of the inter-pulse interval, to interlace the two pulse trains so that the two sub-areas receive alternating laser excitation pulses.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the microscope.

claim: Electrically tunable lenses (ETLs) in the FPUs allow independent focusing of each sub-area.
source: Independent focusing is achieved with electrically tunable lenses (ETLs) in the FPUs (Grewe et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the technical implementation for independent focusing, supported by citation.

claim: ETL focusing provides a z-range of up to 600 µm.
source: In combination with a 6-mm pair of scan mirrors, ETL focusing provides a z-range of up to 600 µm.
evidence: This is a technical specification of the microscope's axial range.

claim: Approximately 150 neurons per sub-area were imaged across ~1800 trials over 5–6 experimental sessions.
source: Using this approach, we imaged in 7 mice ~150 neurons per sub-area (distributed over three imaging planes at different cortical depths) across ~1800 trials over 5–6 experimental sessions.
evidence: This describes the scale of the imaging experiments performed.

claim: In total, 228 S1S2, 817 S1ND, 193 S2S1, and 750 S2ND neurons were imaged in 63 pairs of focal planes across S1 and S2.
source: In total, 228 S1S2, 817 S1ND, 193 S2S1, and 750 S2ND neurons were imaged in 63 pairs of focal planes across S1 and S2.
evidence: This provides the total number of neurons of each type imaged in the study.

claim: Calcium traces were denoised using tensor decomposition to improve statistical analysis of single-trial responses.
source: In order to improve statistical analysis of single-trial responses for trial conditions with low trial numbers, calcium traces were denoised using tensor decomposition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the data processing method used, with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Mice were trained to perform a whisker-based go/no-go texture discrimination task.
source: Animals were habituated to head-fixation and trained to perform a whisker-based go/no-go texture discrimination task (Figure 2D,E) (Chen et al., 2013b; 2015).
evidence: This describes the behavioral task used in the study, supported by figures and citations.

claim: On 'go' trials, animals were rewarded with a water droplet if they correctly licked when presented with a target texture (P100 sandpaper).
source: On 'go' trials, animals were rewarded with a water droplet if they correctly licked ('Hit') when presented with a target texture (a panel of coarse sandpaper, P100).
evidence: This describes the reward contingency for go trials in the behavioral task.

claim: On 'no-go' trials, mice were supposed to withhold licking when presented with non-rewarded, 'non-target' textures (P280, P1200).
source: On 'no-go' trials, mice were supposed to withhold licking ('correct rejection' or 'CR') when presented with one of two non-rewarded, 'non-target' textures of smoother grades (P280, P1200).
evidence: This describes the behavioral contingency for no-go trials.

claim: False alarms on no-go trials were punished with an air puff and a time-out period.
source: Misses on go trials were not rewarded and false alarms ('FA') on no-go trials were punished with an air puff and a time-out period.
evidence: This describes the punishment contingency for false alarms.

claim: Whisker movements were monitored with high-speed videography at 500 Hz.
source: Whisker movements were monitored with high-speed videography (500 Hz) and licking behavior was measured with a piezo film attached to the water spout.
evidence: This describes the methods for monitoring behavior.

claim: Imaging during behavior was performed at a performance level of d' = 2.62 ± 0.15.
source: Imaging during behaviour began following 3–5 training sessions once animals reached a performance level of d' > 1.75 (80% correct) for one session. Imaging under task conditions was performed over the course of 5–6 sessions at a performance level of d' = 2.62 ± 0.15.
evidence: This describes the behavioral performance level during imaging sessions.

claim: Mice were also imaged under non-task conditions in which textures were presented but no reward or punishment delivered.
source: Once sufficient task-related data was acquired, mice were provided with free access to water and then imaged for an additional 5–6 sessions under non-task conditions, in which textures were presented but no reward or punishment delivered.
evidence: This describes the control condition for comparing task-related activity.

claim: Miss trials were excluded from analysis due to their low occurrence (6.7 ± 0.5% of all trials).
source: Due to their low occurrence (6.7 ± 0.5% of all trials), miss trials were excluded from analysis.
evidence: This describes a data exclusion criterion.

claim: Denoising with tensor decomposition better preserves the onset and peak of calcium transients compared to temporal smoothing by a Gaussian filter.
source: In comparing denoising of simulated transients with tensor decomposition against temporal smoothing by a 5-point Gaussian filter, we observed that denoising with tensor decomposition better preserves the onset and peak of calcium transients, resulting in better CC of denoised to ideal traces (Tensor decomposition 0.69 ± 0.01, Gaussian filter: 0.65 ± 0.01, p<1x10-6, Student's t-test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of denoising methods on simulated data shown in the supplementary figure.
